#7046. Teacher prep programs probed in Education Department’s latest anti-DEI push

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The agency said diversification efforts disregard “merit,” but critics say the programs level the playing field for historically excluded candidates.

The U.S. Department of Education opened a string of investigations into teacher preparation programs on Nov. 13, alleging that they discriminate on the basis of race under Title VI or sex under Title IX.

The investigations mark one of the first times the department's Office for Civil Rights has used civil rights protections to challenge diversification efforts in teacher scholarships, hiring, training and recruitment practices.

The programs at the center of the investigations are aimed at recruiting historically underrepresented groups in the teaching profession, such as men and teachers of color.

“Race, national origin, or sex should not decide who will shape America’s next generation, yet many states and universities seem to prioritize recruiting and training ‘minority’ candidates rather than evaluating candidates based solely on merit,” said Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey in a Nov. 13 statement.

“Education agencies and institutions that consider race, national origin, or sex as a means to withhold opportunities in selecting, supporting, and preparing teaching candidates violate federal law and compromise education excellence."

Richey concluded that students should be "judged on their hard work and merit, not prejudged by the color of their skin or their sex.”

EdTrust, a nonprofit that advocates for racial and economic equity in American education, said in a statement to K-12 Dive that the Trump administration is using civil rights protections meant to "dismantle discrimination and expand opportunity" to instead "undermine pathways into teaching for people historically excluded from the profession betrays that purpose."

“The administration’s false divide between ‘merit’ and diversity perpetuates the damaging suggestion that teachers of color are less qualified or less deserving," said Eric Duncan, director of Pre-K-12 policy of EdTrust, in the Nov. 16 statement. "It discounts their skills, expertise, and contributions while ignoring the systemic barriers that have denied talented people opportunities for generations. Scholarships that address those barriers help ensure that family wealth does not determine who can become a teacher."

The Education Department's investigations, Duncan said, "risk turning civil rights enforcement into a tool for preserving the very inequities it should confront.”

CUNY, which houses the NYC Men Teach Program being investigated by the department, said in a statement to K-12 Dive that it was "proud of its role educating the teachers of tomorrow and our programs are open to all students regardless of race, gender or national origin."

According to the city's website, the program was created around 2015 in collaboration with the federal Education Department and then-Mayor Bill de Blasio with the goal of putting an additional 1,000 men of color into the city’s teacher pipeline.

A March 2026 evaluation of the program conducted for the NYC mayor's office by Westat, which provides research services for government agencies, shows that the program contributed over 3,100 new male teachers of color to New York City Public Schools between school years 2015–16 and 2023–24.

The American Association of Colleges for Teacher Education said in a Nov. 16 email to K-12 Dive, “Strengthening and diversifying the educator pipeline is essential to addressing persistent teacher shortages and ensuring every PK-12 student has access to well-prepared, effective teachers. Decades of research confirm that a diverse educator workforce benefits all students academically, socially, and emotionally." AACTE added that it does not comment on active federal inquiries involving specific institutions or state agencies.

While the investigations are some of the first of their kind by OCR, they build on previous efforts by the Trump administration to weed out DEI in teacher preparation programs — especially in the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard.

Some of the earliest federal grants terminated in 2025 by the administration were under the Supporting Effective Educator Development Grant Program, the Teacher Quality Partnership Program and the Teacher and School Leader Incentive Program, due to what it said was the promotion of "divisive ideologies". The department admitted in a March court filing that it had cancelled 104 out of 109 active TQP and SEED grants.

The loss of over 100 federal teacher training grants last year caused at least 127 teacher candidates to drop out of their programs and another 259 accepted candidates to not enroll after all, according to survey findings released in October.

Those cuts were preceded by an anti-DEI directive that has since been heavily litigated and was most recently blocked in court in September.

That anti-DEI letter specifically called for agency personnel to review all new grant awards and issued grants to ensure those federal dollars “do not fund discriminatory practices — including in the form of DEI.” The directive added that “Illegal DEI policies and practices can violate both the letter and purpose of Federal civil rights law and conflict with the Department’s policy of prioritizing merit, fairness, and excellence in education.”

The Justice Department in August 2025 also warned districts they could be exposed to legal liability by asking job applicants how their “cultural background informs their teaching,” using recruitment strategies targeting candidates from specific geographic areas or racial backgrounds, and asking job candidates to describe how they overcame obstacles.

Since the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, civil rights groups have raised concerns that it would set back educational equity efforts even outside of race-conscious admissions. That decision undid race-conscious policies in college admissions, and the Education Department under Trump has used it to justify scaling back other diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives in education.

Scholarship availability, teacher pipelines and student affinity groups were among the top areas beyond college access that advocates were concerned could be impacted in the wake of the ruling.

Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss

#7035. Lawsuit alleges chronic underfunding of University of Maryland Eastern Shore

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A group of students, faculty and alumni said the historically Black institution has been discriminated against and shortchanged $6 billion since its founding.

The plaintiffs are two UMES students and a corporate entity created last year called ForUMES, which, according to the complaint, is made up of university faculty, students, alumni and prospects and is aimed at bolstering the “educational, research, public service, and charitable objectives for UMES.”

The plaintiffs described UMES as “the woefully underfunded stepchild of the University System of Maryland.”

The complaint traces the funding disparity back to 1890, when Maryland wanted to take advantage of the federal Second Morrill Act.

That law sought to bolster the country’s land-grant universities with additional annual funding. But the money wasn’t available for states whose public land-grant institutions had racially discriminatory admissions unless they had a comparable college “of like character” for Black students, per the statute.

According to the lawsuit, Henry Alvord — who was then the president of University of Maryland, College Park, the state’s first land-grant institution — was “in a dilemma.”

The university “was in desperate need of additional funding but the idea of permitting Black students to attend [UMD] was unfathomable because his and many others’ racist beliefs would never allow [UMD] to be integrated,” the lawsuit states.

Alvord eventually found a solution to his dilemma in the Princess Anne Academy, a “small, remote and run-down preparatory school on the southern point of the eastern shore” that could — on paper — become a land-grant college for Black students, operated by Morgan College, which later became the HBCU Morgan State University.

However, the “lion’s share” of the new funding under the Second Morrill Act went to UMD, which did not admit Black students until a 1950 lawsuit.

“Black students would be sent to far-off Princess Anne to receive junior and senior high school-level classes on Princess Anne Academy’s dilapidated campus instead of a school of ‘like character’ to [UMD]’s state-of-the-art college,” plaintiffs said in the complaint.

According to the lawsuit, the underfunding and neglect of the academy — which later became UMES — continued throughout the 20th century and amid regular federal scrutiny of segregation in Maryland’s higher educational system and disparately low funding for UMES.

In 2023, then-President Joe Biden’s secretaries of education and agriculture wrote to Maryland Gov. Wes Moore — who is named as a defendant in the new lawsuit along with other top officials — to address the historical funding disparities at UMES as part of a broader effort to encourage more funding at historically Black land-grant colleges across the country.

“The longstanding and ongoing underinvestment in University of Maryland Eastern Shore disadvantages the students, faculty, and community that the institution serves,” the Biden officials wrote. “Furthermore, it may contribute to a lack of economic activity that would ultimately benefit Maryland.”

They calculated that UMES had been underfunded to the tune of $321.2 million just over the prior 30 years before the letter.

“These funds could have supported infrastructure and student services and would have better positioned the university to compete for research grants,” they said, while also acknowledging that “your state budget has taken steps to address this historic underinvestment.”

Since 2023, UMES has received around $9 million a year in additional state funding through a landmark Maryland law passed in 2021 aimed at expanding support for the state’s HBCUs and settling a lawsuit brought by the institutions’ supporters.

Enrollment has also been on the increase at the university. In fall 2024, UMES had 3,177 students, up 10.1% from five years prior, according to federal data.

The lawsuit’s plaintiffs don’t say how they calculated the $6 billion in damages they are seeking for UMES. In addition to monetary reparation for the years of underfunding, they asked the judge to require state officials to allocate land-grant funding equitably between UMD and UMES.

#7032. Supreme Court declines Trump bid to revive DEI research funding cuts

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A lower court blocked the administration from pulling funding from University of California researchers over project topics it opposed.

Shortly after President Donald Trump retook office early last year, federal agencies began slashing federal research funding en masse, often with little warning or explanation.

The UC researchers sued the administration in June 2025, arguing, in part, that the grant terminations violated their First Amendment rights by targeting their work based on viewpoint.

Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation later confirmed in court documents that they cut UC-affiliated grants if they “expressed, or were presumed to express, viewpoints disfavored by the Administration.”

They said they made decisions via keyword searches for terms like “diversity” and “health equity.” NIH also said it canceled some grants because they had previously been awarded diversity supplements, additional funding meant to support researchers from underrepresented and disadvantaged backgrounds.

The Trump administration took the case to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which sided with the researchers.

In the Trump administration’s request to the Supreme Court, federal attorneys said that the appeals court’s ruling erroneously “interferes with executive-branch priorities in spending taxpayer funds” and establishes “dangerous precedent that will hamstring every future administration when seeking to subsidize private projects that promote view-points aligned with government policy.”

The high court did not address those arguments this week. Its decision paves the way for UC to have its funding fully restored, a process that is already underway.

For example, Farella Braun + Martel, one of the legal firms representing the plaintiffs, said in September that its lawyers reached a settlement agreement with the Environmental Protection Agency to permanently restore $19 million in canceled UC research grants. A hearing on the motion to approve the agreement is scheduled for next month.

#7030. Trump taps DEI opponent to lead DOJ’s civil rights division

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

While at the U.S. Department of Education, Craig Trainor threatened to strip federal funding from schools over their diversity initiatives.

The selection of Trainor, who the Justice Department said is entering the position in “an acting capacity,” signals that the Trump administration isn’t backing away from its heavy crackdown on schools and their diversity initiatives. Trainor is set to replace Harmeet Dhillon, one of several top DOJ officials who stepped down after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections.

Under Dhillon, the department’s civil rights division aggressively pursued schools and states over LGBTQ+ policies — such as transgender student inclusion on sports teams and parental notification of students' gender identity concerns. Additionally, the division has pursued race-related investigations into programs meant to be inclusive of historically marginalized students, and it lifted a number of decades-old desegregation orders.

The Justice Department also joined a lawsuit in February against the Los Angeles Unified School District over a court-ordered desegregation program.

During Dhillon’s tenure, the agency entered an interagency agreement with the Education Department, taking on some civil rights investigation duties that were previously housed within the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights.

Since then, the two agencies rescinded at least seven documents related to English learner and other minority protections on the grounds that they were "not enforceable." Trainor has likewise spearheaded major efforts to stamp out DEI in K-12. While serving as the Education Department’s acting assistant secretary for civil rights, Trainor threatened in February 2025 guidance to pull federal funding from schools over DEI initiatives that it said amounted to "race-based decisionmaking."

The letter said "a school may not use students’ personal essays, writing samples, participation in extracurriculars, or other cues" as a proxy for race in issues "pertaining to admissions, hiring, promotion, compensation, financial aid, scholarships, prizes, administrative support, discipline, housing, graduation ceremonies, and all other aspects of student, academic, and campus life."

Federal judges have struck down the guidance. However, the DOJ released similar sweeping guidance last year that threatens to strip federal grant funding from schools over what the agency deems as illegal DEI. DOJ officials flagged several commonplace practices as potentially unlawful, ranging from requiring job applicants how their “cultural background informs their teaching,” using recruitment strategies targeting candidates from specific geographic areas or racial backgrounds, and asking job candidates to describe how they overcame obstacles.

Trainor pursued similar anti-DEI policies in his most recent appointment as the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s assistant secretary for fair housing and equal opportunity, a position he was confirmed for by the Senate in October 2025. In that role, Trainor issued guidance warning colleges that affinity housing may violate federal law.

#7021. Teacher prep programs probed in Education Department’s latest anti-DEI push

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The agency said diversification efforts disregard “merit,” but critics say the programs level the playing field for historically excluded candidates.

The U.S. Department of Education opened a string of investigations into teacher preparation programs on Nov. 13, alleging that they discriminate on the basis of race under Title VI or sex under Title IX.

The investigations mark one of the first times the department's Office for Civil Rights has used civil rights protections to challenge diversification efforts in teacher scholarships, hiring, training and recruitment practices.

The programs at the center of the investigations are aimed at recruiting historically underrepresented groups in the teaching profession, such as men and teachers of color.

“Race, national origin, or sex should not decide who will shape America’s next generation, yet many states and universities seem to prioritize recruiting and training ‘minority’ candidates rather than evaluating candidates based solely on merit,” said Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey in a Nov. 13 statement.

“Education agencies and institutions that consider race, national origin, or sex as a means to withhold opportunities in selecting, supporting, and preparing teaching candidates violate federal law and compromise education excellence."

Richey concluded that students should be "judged on their hard work and merit, not prejudged by the color of their skin or their sex.”

EdTrust, a nonprofit that advocates for racial and economic equity in American education, said in a statement to K-12 Dive that the Trump administration is using civil rights protections meant to "dismantle discrimination and expand opportunity" to instead "undermine pathways into teaching for people historically excluded from the profession betrays that purpose."

“The administration’s false divide between ‘merit’ and diversity perpetuates the damaging suggestion that teachers of color are less qualified or less deserving," said Eric Duncan, director of Pre-K-12 policy of EdTrust, in the Nov. 16 statement. "It discounts their skills, expertise, and contributions while ignoring the systemic barriers that have denied talented people opportunities for generations. Scholarships that address those barriers help ensure that family wealth does not determine who can become a teacher."

The Education Department's investigations, Duncan said, "risk turning civil rights enforcement into a tool for preserving the very inequities it should confront.”

CUNY, which houses the NYC Men Teach Program being investigated by the department, said in a statement to K-12 Dive that it was "proud of its role educating the teachers of tomorrow and our programs are open to all students regardless of race, gender or national origin."

According to the city's website, the program was created around 2015 in collaboration with the federal Education Department and then-Mayor Bill de Blasio with the goal of putting an additional 1,000 men of color into the city’s teacher pipeline.

A March 2026 evaluation of the program conducted for the NYC mayor's office by Westat, which provides research services for government agencies, shows that the program contributed over 3,100 new male teachers of color to New York City Public Schools between school years 2015–16 and 2023–24.

The American Association of Colleges for Teacher Education said in a Nov. 16 email to K-12 Dive, “Strengthening and diversifying the educator pipeline is essential to addressing persistent teacher shortages and ensuring every PK-12 student has access to well-prepared, effective teachers. Decades of research confirm that a diverse educator workforce benefits all students academically, socially, and emotionally." AACTE added that it does not comment on active federal inquiries involving specific institutions or state agencies.

While the investigations are some of the first of their kind by OCR, they build on previous efforts by the Trump administration to weed out DEI in teacher preparation programs — especially in the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard.

Some of the earliest federal grants terminated in 2025 by the administration were under the Supporting Effective Educator Development Grant Program, the Teacher Quality Partnership Program and the Teacher and School Leader Incentive Program, due to what it said was the promotion of "divisive ideologies". The department admitted in a March court filing that it had cancelled 104 out of 109 active TQP and SEED grants.

The loss of over 100 federal teacher training grants last year caused at least 127 teacher candidates to drop out of their programs and another 259 accepted candidates to not enroll after all, according to survey findings released in October.

Those cuts were preceded by an anti-DEI directive that has since been heavily litigated and was most recently blocked in court in September.

That anti-DEI letter specifically called for agency personnel to review all new grant awards and issued grants to ensure those federal dollars “do not fund discriminatory practices — including in the form of DEI.” The directive added that “Illegal DEI policies and practices can violate both the letter and purpose of Federal civil rights law and conflict with the Department’s policy of prioritizing merit, fairness, and excellence in education.”

The Justice Department in August 2025 also warned districts they could be exposed to legal liability by asking job applicants how their “cultural background informs their teaching,” using recruitment strategies targeting candidates from specific geographic areas or racial backgrounds, and asking job candidates to describe how they overcame obstacles.

Since the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, civil rights groups have raised concerns that it would set back educational equity efforts even outside of race-conscious admissions. That decision undid race-conscious policies in college admissions, and the Education Department under Trump has used it to justify scaling back other diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives in education.

Scholarship availability, teacher pipelines and student affinity groups were among the top areas beyond college access that advocates were concerned could be impacted in the wake of the ruling.

Spanberger decided to pivot away from participating in the first nationwide federal school choice tax credit program because it does not appear it would benefit students in Virginia public schools, the governor’s office spokesperson said in a Monday statement.

“Public money should go to public education,” the spokesperson said.

As of Nov. 13, the IRS reported that 31 states — including Virginia — had indicated their desire to participate in the first federal school choice tax credit program available nationwide. The list still excludes New York despite Gov. Kathy Hochul announcing in October that the state would opt in.

With the midterm elections earlier this month resulting in six state governorships flipping from Republican to Democrat in Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, it’s possible that more last-minute changes to stop participating in the Education Freedom Tax Credit, such as in Virginia, could unfold over the next few months. All six states with newly elected Democratic governors have already opted into the program.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit program was approved by the Republican-led Congress in July 2025 when it was included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and signed into law by President Donald Trump.

The scholarships — generated through taxpayer donations to SGOs — could go toward both private school tuition and public school expenses like tutoring, ed tech and services for students with disabilities.

Supporters tout that the program will expand education opportunities for students. Critics, however, push back that the program is a threat to public school funding and will mostly benefit wealthy families.

The Virginia Education Association, a statewide union of teachers and school support professionals, in a Monday statement praised Spanberger for her decision to step away from the Education Freedom Tax Credit. The union said it estimated that Virginia public schools could have lost $1 billion annually if the state had moved forward in its participation in the program.

“Ample evidence tells us that voucher programs are damaging to public schools and students, draining resources from already underfunded school systems,” said VEA President Carol Bauer in a statement. “VEA members applaud Governor Spanberger’s wisdom in opting the Commonwealth out of the federal voucher program, the future of which is in limbo anyway as a new Congress takes over early next year.”

Meanwhile, Steven Cheeseman, president and CEO of the National Catholic Educational Association, said in a Saturday statement that he was “deeply disappointed” and “frankly shocked” about Virginia’s decision to no longer participate in the federal scholarship tax credit program. He urged Spanberger to reconsider and continue completing the opt-in process.

“This is a stunning step backward for Virginia families. Walking away from this program puts politics ahead of the more than one million students in Virginia public schools who will miss out on support for tutoring, school supplies, educational technology, and after-school care,” Cheeseman said.

Christian Education Network Founder Aaron Baer called Spanberger's decision “potentially illegal.” Baer added that the legal teams at Christian Education Network and Virginia Christian Education Network are “actively evaluating the governor’s actions.”

“Families should have the freedom to choose the education that best meets their children's needs, regardless of their income or ZIP code. Denying them access to these scholarships is a direct attack on that freedom,” Baer said in a Monday statement.

#7015. DHS’ 4-year cap on student visa stays struck down by federal judge

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The law does not grant the agency “such broad and open-ended authority to undermine” the student visa program, the judge wrote.

DHS published the rule in July, arguing it was needed to protect national security and prevent visa fraud. International students would have been able to seek extensions on their visas, but the decision would have been at federal officials’ sole discretion.

The rule would have changed long-standing policy permitting foreign students to stay in the U.S. for as long as it takes to complete their academic studies.

Several higher ed groups and unions, including the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration and the American Federation of Teachers, sued the agency in August over the regulations.

Saylor handed the plaintiffs an early win when he temporarily blocked the visa cap from taking effect. Writing that they were likely to succeed in their case, the judge flagged that the rule could be abused by the Trump administration.

“It is not difficult to imagine how that system might be abused to punish those whose viewpoints or research are disfavored by the officials making the decision — or, indeed, punish disfavored institutions,” Saylor said in his Sept. 14 order.

He repeated those concerns Monday, describing the student visa process DHS sought to set up as an “unreviewable, completely discretionary renewal system.”

Saylor further said DHS failed to weigh “less burdensome” options.

The DHS rule would have done more than limit student visa stays. Some international students would have been barred from changing their field of study or transferring colleges. And they could not come to the U.S. to pursue an academic degree at the same or a lower level than a degree they already possess.

For example, an international student who holds a law degree would effectively be banned from pursuing a master’s degree in the U.S., Saylor said.

“Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity — providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States — that Congress sought to permit and encourage,” he said. “The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority” to undermine the student visa program.

The judge’s decision may not put the case to bed, as the Trump administration could still appeal it. The continued uncertainty comes as new data shows a decline in international enrollment in the U.S.

In 2025-26, the number of foreign students attending U.S. colleges dropped 2.7% year over year, according to the latest Open Doors report. And preliminary data from fall 2026 found that international enrollment declined another 9% annually at surveyed institutions. Both decreases were driven by losses of new students and those pursuing graduate degrees.

#7008. Are strict school cellphone bans working?

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Schools requiring devices to be locked in pouches saw gains equal to as much as two weeks of additional instruction per year, a Harvard study finds.

Expanded access to broadband cellphones appeared to occur around the same time student achievement began a slow but steady long-term decline beginning in 2013, the Harvard study said.

For teens, the research noted that access to cellphones grew quickly, from 23% of 13- to 17-year-olds having smartphones in 2011 to 95% by 2018.

Every year since about 2013, U.S. students have lost two to three weeks of learning, said Tom Kane, a Harvard professor and one of the leading authors of the study, in a Tuesday statement.

“It’s been a slow leak that, over time, has put U.S. 8th graders almost a year behind. Strict cell phone bans seem to plug about half of that leak,” Kane said.

This research comes as states increasingly adopt policies to restrict cellphone use in schools and as student test scores on the National Assessment of Educational Progress continue to disappoint, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. Twenty-two states require bell-to-bell cellphone bans as of Oct. 29, according to a tracker by the National Council of School Safety Directors.

The Harvard study’s findings differ from another key report by the National Bureau of Economic Research released earlier this year on the impact of cellphone pouches.

That NBER study said there was little effect on academic achievement three years after schools adopted cellphone pouches. Researchers, however, found an 80% drop in students’ reported cellphone use once personal device pouch policies were in place. Part of the NBER study included an analysis of GPS “pings” on cellphones from 40,542 schools between January 2019 and January 2026.

At the same time, a survey shared by The Brookings Institution in September reported that nearly half of teens ages 13-17 said their teachers' enforcement of cellphone restrictions waned over the course of the 2025-26 school year. Researchers from the Center for Applied Research in Education — part of the University of Southern California’s Center for Economic and Social Research — who analyzed the survey findings concluded that bell-to-bell policies may be more durable to implement in schools versus less-strict cellphone policies.

#7007. School bus driver shortage worsens again, as hourly wages dip

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Districts face cuts to bus routes, increased safety risks and other hardships when they’re short on drivers, the Economic Policy Institute said.

EPI's analysis included school bus drivers employed by privately contracted firms and those employed directly by districts.

There were nearly 15% fewer school bus drivers employed at the start of this school year compared to September 2019. Private sector school bus driver employment fell 35.9% over the same period, while state and local government bus driver employment declined 9.2%, the EPI report said.

Hourly wages for school bus drivers as of Sept. 1, 2026, were $22.49, a 0.7% drop compared to the same date last year. Meanwhile, overall bus driver hourly wages as of Sept. 1, 2026, were $23.89.

But even with the lower hourly wages for school bus drivers, inflation-adjusted median weekly wages rose 3.9% year-over-year. The EPI report said this may be because school bus drivers are working longer shifts or driving extra days to make up for employment shortages. This, however, is not a long-term solution for districts with school bus driver shortages, because it could lead to an overworked driving staff, EPI said.

EPI points to several factors that are negatively impacting districts’ abilities to pay more competitive wages for school bus drivers. Those include the expiration of federal COVID-19 emergency relief funds, ongoing federal and state funding cuts, and the expansion of private school choice.

Additionally, increased costs like higher diesel prices are straining public school budgets, the report said.

"If state and local lawmakers want the children in their regions to get to school on time, have reliable access to after-school programs, and otherwise attend healthy, supportive schools, then they must provide stronger funding for public schools and better pay for school staff," the report said.

#7003. ABA accreditation arm moves to nix full-time faculty standard for first-year classes

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The U.S. Department of Justice recently threatened an antitrust probe over the requirement, arguing that it drives up legal education costs.

The ABA’s accreditation council voted to eliminate the standard while under pressure from the Justice Department. In an October letter, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said the group could face an antitrust investigation if it didn’t eliminate the full-time faculty requirement, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Woodward argued that adjunct faculty are less expensive to hire and often have more firsthand experience, and that limiting their role in first-year law school education drives up costs and hurts students, the Journal reported.

The accreditation council also plans to seek public comment on further potential changes to its policies regarding full-time instructors that are meant to provide more flexibility to law schools.

The council is in communication with the Justice Department, a spokesperson for the council said Tuesday. The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

Woodward’s letter came after the ABA’s accreditation council began seeking public comment in September on proposed changes to its full-time faculty requirements.

The accreditation council’s proposals drew mixed reactions from law schools and professors.

In a public comment, the faculty leadership of the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school opposed nixing the requirement regarding the first year of curriculum.

They argued that the first-year of law school “is a key period for educating students on core legal principles, doctrines, and analytical methods” and “a critically important time for creating community among law school students.”

“Full-time faculty are simply more available for answering student questions outside of class, as it is part of their full-time job to do so,” the faculty leaders wrote. “And perhaps most importantly, full-time faculty build pedagogical expertise in designing courses, sequencing learning, assessing progress, and giving constructive feedback.”

Yet others voiced support for the change. Terence Lau, dean of Syracuse University’s law school, argued that the changes would reduce “undue burden” while still preserving full-time faculty members’ “core role” in legal education.

Lau argued the current standard limits the ability for law schools to tap sitting judges or emeritus professors for first-year instruction. “Law schools should be able to draw on these teachers where they best serve students,” he wrote.

Last week’s vote comes as the accreditation council is under the microscope by the Trump administration.

In August, a report from U.S. Department of Education staffers recommended that the agency strip the ABA’s accreditation council of federal recognition. The staffers concluded that the council wasn’t compliant with over two dozen federal criteria and alleged that it wasn’t sufficiently independent from the ABA’s professional organization.

Losing federal recognition would mean the ABA’s accreditation council could no longer serve as a gatekeeper to Title IV financial aid. Although the group accredits some 200 law schools, only five rely on it for access to federal aid, a council representative said in September to a federal advisory panel reviewing the department’s findings.

That panel, which advises the Education Department on accreditation matters, deadlocked on a vote on whether to recommend that the council lose recognition. Education Under Secretary Nicholas Kent is soon expected to make a final call on the matter.

The ABA’s accreditation council has also caught flak from the Trump administration over its prior diversity standard. The council formally repealed the standard in September after suspending it in February 2025.

#7002. How can districts keep CTE programs relevant as tech evolves?

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The rapid pace of change can make it difficult for even employers to have clear answers for workplace readiness, an industry expert says.

How can leaders of high school career and technical education programs ensure those offerings remain relevant in preparing students to adapt in a rapidly changing workforce?

“That question is one everyone is trying to answer right now. I’m not sure there is one clear answer,” said Alisha Hyslop, chief policy, research and content officer at the Association for Career and Technical Education.

Hyslop said the main piece of advice for educators is to work closely with businesses and industries to ensure programs are preparing students with the skills they’ll need to be successful — and that’s probably the same, at least on the surface, as it would have been 10 or 20 years ago.

But there are important distinctions in 2026, Hyslop said.

Because technology is changing so rapidly, employers don’t always have a clear answer for workplace readiness approaches, she said.

Hyslop said ACTE is also hearing that students need to understand basic, foundational artificial intelligence skills and how to use them. Additionally, students should continue to "build up durable skills," which is "really critical," she said.

Despite employers’ own lack of clarity at times, regular conversations should definitely continue, Hyslop said.

“There should be a give-and-take between the CTE educators, and folks working on curriculum and instruction in CTE, and the employer community,” she said. And although technology will continue to rapidly evolve, “students are still going to need critical thinking and communications skills, and the ability to work in teams, and evaluate information — and all of those foundational skills that apply across technologies.”

CTE programs focused on information technology are changing the most rapidly, although Hyslop said she has seen plenty of research to show that across the spectrum of career fields, new AI tools are being implemented and deployed. One example is the use of the technology in the agriculture field to monitor soil health and predict crop growth, she said.

“We had some examples from a school in Bentonville [Ark.] that was using AI in health science programs. They had created a meal planning app for mothers with gestational diabetes, or for pregnant women who could get answers to specific questions; those were joint projects between healthcare and technology students," Hyslop said. "There were lots of applications in digital media, and lots of ethical considerations that students are exploring as they go through that process.”

While some industries are more impacted by the advent of AI and other changes in the workplace than others, at first glance, people might think it’s mainly an issue in technology classes, Hyslop said. “And that is not the case. Because we’re seeing applications across career areas, once students get into the workplace.”

During a panel discussion at a recent ACTE conference focused on the use of AI in CTE programs, Hyslop said, students emphasized how important it was that they learned foundational skills first.

One student pointed out the approach of using a calculator to solve math problems, she recalled. “But that’s not how we teach students in kindergarten. We teach them basic mathematical functions first, and then introduce the calculator to do more complicated things.”

By learning the foundational level skills in CTE programs, they could evaluate the answers given by AI more competently, the students said. For instance, a student studying automotive mechanics could examine AI-generated instructions on how to fix cars.

“If you had no real understanding of those instructions, you wouldn’t know if it made a mistake,” she said. “That was a really important takeaway from that panel — that even students realized that AI, or whatever the next technology is, is still going to need people to instruct, evaluate and modify all of these technologies.”

#7001. PASSHE moves to close Commonwealth University’s Mansfield campus

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The public college system’s leader said the campus faces persistent deficits and long-running enrollment declines.

The push to close Commonwealth’s Mansfield campus comes nearly two years after the university moved to eliminate its smallest campus in Clearfield, which is set to close after the current academic year.

Mansfield’s closure would leave Commonwealth with two campuses — its main location in Bloomsburg and one in Lock Haven. The university was created in 2022 out of the merger of Bloomsburg, Lock Haven and Mansfield universities.

In justifying his decision to shutter Mansfield, Fiorentino cited cratering headcounts as well as persistent financial losses and local demographic shifts. He presented these factors as a drag on the university and PASSHE as a whole.

Between 2009 and 2026, Commonwealth’s Mansfield campus fall headcount plummeted 71.6% to 1,013 students, according to PASSHE data.

That count is projected to drop by another 200-plus students by fall 2028 amid declining first-year student enrollment and second-year retention rates, according to data in Fiorentino’s letter. He also pointed to estimates of falling high school graduate numbers in the surrounding counties.

“Fewer new students are enrolling at the Mansfield campus, reducing tuition revenue and putting additional pressure on the university's finances,” the PASSHE chancellor wrote to Osgood.

Fiorentino pointed to state funding meant to help Mansfield, including $75 million in one-time money used in part to clear the campus’s debt. And still the campus’s unrestricted deficit grew to $7.7 million for fiscal 2026.

Closing the campus would “reduce the likelihood that Commonwealth University would need to draw upon the reserves held by the other PASSHE universities,” Fiorentino said.

But a faculty union blasted the plan. Kenneth Mash, president of the Association of Pennsylvania State College and University Faculties, said in a statement Tuesday that closing Mansfield would “ravage public higher education in Pennsylvania, create additional higher-education deserts, and hurt students.”

“This news came as a surprise, and it is unfortunate that the System has decided to approach this plan clandestinely,” Mash said. “We will not let Pennsylvania give up on our commitment to provide the opportunity for our students to earn a high-quality, low-cost public higher education. We will fight for Mansfield.”

On a FAQ page, PASSHE said it anticipates layoffs at the Mansfield campus but that it will adhere to collective bargaining agreements and “work to minimize the impact on university employees.”

As part of the wind-down plan for Mansfield, Fiorentino directed Osgood to detail arrangements for the campus's current students to finish their degrees with Commonwealth.

Commonwealth as a whole faces a $17 million operating deficit and recently announced that it could slash 175 jobs to help close the budget gap.

The university isn’t alone in its struggles — even in Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania State University is implementing a plan to shutter seven of its regional Commonwealth campuses to shore up the university’s central budget and cut losses in areas with declining enrollment.

#6998. 29 states will require finance course in high school by 2031, report predicts

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Ten states received an “A” for requiring standalone personal finance courses in the National Endowment for Financial Education’s latest report.

“We’re excited about the progress this year’s report shows,” said Taylor Stanek, managing director of policy and advocacy for NEFE. “There is momentum and movement behind the effort to create a national expectation that students receive financial education in high school.”

The center's research involved reviews of each states' approach to personal finance education in high schools, state academic standards on the topic, and related laws, guidelines and regulations.

Broadly speaking, states with an “A” grade have shown they are implementing financial education with fidelity, while those receiving a “B” or “C” offer some level of financial education but short of a full semester course. These states also may have some degree of requirements in statewide academic standards.

States receiving a “D” or “F” have little or nothing to offer at the moment, Stanek said, expressing optimism that all 50 states will receive an “A” eventually.

“There are a few things we are keeping a close eye on as states move forward,” he said. “Implementation is key; passing one of these requirements is just a start."

The states also need to make sure schools are offering the courses as expected, as a standalone commitment, with teachers who have been trained, and have curricular materials available to meet the needs of specific students, Stanek said.

"This is an opportunity for every state … to make sure they’re evaluating the effectiveness of these programs and maximizing their benefit and impact,” Stanek said. Each state takes a somewhat different approach based on their unique range of needs, he added.

Utah implemented the first semester-long financial education requirement in 2008 and conducts statewide audits on programs, while Missouri was the second state in 2010, Stanek said. Even states with “C” grades or lower have seen progress in certain localities, with Denver Public Schools adopting this ahead of the state of Colorado, for example, he said.

“In the majority of other states, there’s at least something in place,” he added. “It’s ensuring that it’s offered across the board — requiring it to make sure every student receives it. When it’s an elective, students of color, low-income students and female students are less likely to take it.”

The figures from the 2025 national opinion poll underscore why the momentum has grown, especially at a time of economic uncertainty, Stanek said. “There’s a recognition that people need extra support to be [financially] successful,” he said.

“This is no longer a niche side topic. Folks are saying this is something worthy of being a core academic discipline in our K-12 system.”

The previous five editions of the report were published by the Center for Financial Literacy at Champlain College in Burlington, Vt.

#6996. Fewer than half of students are kindergarten-ready, GAO says

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A five-state analysis shows girls, as well as Asian and White children, were more prepared. Boys, Black students and those with disabilities were less so.

Positive factors associated with kindergarten readiness include parenting, home environment and students' learning-related skills and social behaviors. Negative factors may include health, socioeconomic status, gender, and race or ethnicity, the Nov. 12 report said.

GAO's analysis of seven of the 11 studies found that public preschool programs had different impacts on varying student demographic groups when compared to students who didn't attend such programs. For instance, in one Georgia district, a publicly funded preschool program led to "persistently positive effects" for children from lower-income families.

The five states studied — Connecticut, Florida, Kentucky, Maryland and Ohio — also showed variation in kindergarten readiness rates. That may be due in part to how the states measure readiness, administer their kindergarten entry assessments, or report the assessment results, GAO said.

Among the five states, kindergarten readiness rates also differed by district type. Suburban districts were generally closer to their state's average for kindergarten readiness, while rural and urban districts varied more.

Also at the local level, the analysis found better kindergarten readiness rates among school districts in Connecticut, Kentucky and Ohio that had higher rates of students enrolled in public or private preschool. But there was no statistically significant association in that regard in Florida or Maryland.

This month's GAO report follows a 2024 report from the government watchdog agency on how states and teachers use kindergarten readiness data.

The 2024-25 school year saw record highs in enrollment and funding for state-supported preschool nationwide, according to The State of Preschool 2025, a report released earlier this year by the National Institute for Early Education Research. However, the rate of enrollment growth slowed compared to the 2023-24 school year, and many states still were not back to pre-pandemic preschool enrollment rates, the NIEER report said.

#6994. Court blocks DHS policy limiting international student training opportunities

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The higher education groups suing to strike down new limits on the Curricular Practical Training program are likely to succeed, a federal judge ruled.

The lawsuit was brought by prominent higher education groups, including the Association of American Universities. They argued that DHS unlawfully changed decades of “settled agency interpretation” when it issued its new two memos.

DHS pushed back in court documents, arguing that the two memos didn’t alter “the legal regime” because they were simply reminders about the CPT program’s regulatory requirements. However, Kobick wrote that they “represent a marked departure” from the agency’s prior interpretation.

Since 1991, the federal government has allowed international students to qualify for training opportunities — even if they weren’t mandated by their degree program — so long as they resulted in academic credit, Kobick wrote.

Yet in the August memos, DHS put new restrictions on the CPT program without acknowledging that it was shifting long-standing federal policy. Under its interpretation, an international student could only participate in a training opportunity like an internship if it was required of all students in their degree program.

“In practice, for example, this meant that a law school could not authorize CPT for a law student on an F-1 visa to extern for a federal judge for academic credit unless such an externship was required of all students seeking to earn a juris doctor degree,” Kobick wrote.

DHS also threatened college officials with civil and criminal liability if they didn’t comply with the memos.

Many colleges responded to the two memos by rejecting or revoking CPT authorization for some of their international students or by adjusting their program requirements.

At Columbia University, in New York, officials denied CPT authorization to over 120 international students this fall, according to court documents. Similarly, over a dozen international students at Grinnell College, in Iowa, lost out on internships due to the change.

Some colleges — including Cornell and Michigan State universities — reported that they’ve lost international students due to the two directives. And college officials have reported reluctance to sign documents related to the program over fear of being prosecuted.

A spokesperson for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which operates under DHS, said in an email Wednesday that it does not comment on pending litigation.

Science-backed. Design-led. AI-powered. Global.

We’re not looking for someone who only advises on what to test, we’re looking for someone who builds it. A hands-on Head of Growth who can ideate, write the copy, design the strategy and launch experiments directly.

1. Generate hypotheses. Read the signals (ad performance, webinar attendance, sales calls, objections, churn reasons, comments, competitors’ ads) and propose what to test next, with a cost and an expected impact.

2. Act across every tool. Not a chatbot in a tab: it reads and writes in our whole stack, from ad accounts to CRM, landing pages, webinars, email, social DMs and analytics.

3. Hold the full context of Paradox. Our DNA, offers, voice, member stories, past campaigns and what they taught us, in one shared company brain.

4. Ship its hypotheses. Produce the hook, the ad cut, the page, the email sequence or the funnel variant, and put it live.

5. Measure with real KPIs. Every test is tied to a number that matters (cost per qualified lead, show-up rate, close rate, CAC, payback, LTV), not to likes or reach.

6. Learn and loop on its own. Scale what works, kill what doesn’t, write the lesson back into the brain, and launch the next cycle without waiting for a meeting.

This is already real. Our growth hub tracks every hypothesis and experiment, with its result. An ads library of thousands of creatives feeds our creative research. Agents cut ads from long-form content, prepare webinars, wire Instagram comment-to-DM automations and audit our tracking after every live. Athena, our AI coach, works with members every day.

We believe self-help is broken: generic theory, a quick high, no real change.

We believe people deserve more. More than content. More than motivation.

They deserve a system that knows them, one that adapts, challenges, and grows with them.

Growth at Paradox means bringing people into something that actually changes their life, and proving it.

- Human Intelligence (coaches, peers, and mentors)

- Structured Intelligence (protocols, mental models, rituals)

- Technological Intelligence (AI personalization, feedback loops, adaptive journeys)

To create one seamless ecosystem: Paradox OS.

Paradox was founded by David Laroche, a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson and Gad Elmaleh. We started in French. We’re building for the world.

Here’s the bet: a company that learns by itself grows in a way a company of people alone can’t. A small growth team running a self-learning machine can out-test, out-learn and out-grow teams a hundred times its size.

We hold ourselves to the standards of Apple, Spotify and MasterClass. While others hide their numbers, we let our results speak.

As Head of Growth, you’ll be the architect of a growth machine that learns by itself. In a classic growth team, people do the work and AI helps. Here it’s the other way round: agents do the work, you design the system, set the bar and make the calls.

You don’t just manage a team, you get your hands dirty to identify growth levers and pull them yourself.

❌ The old way: a Head of Growth hires people and agencies, briefs them, and checks their work.

🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: your team is mostly agents, and you build them yourself. You write their skills, plug them into our tools (ad accounts, CRM, webinars, email, analytics) and write the evals that tell an agent what "good" means: a hook that stops the scroll, a page that converts, a test that’s worth its cost.

You give autonomy step by step: first an agent suggests, then it acts once you approve, then it acts alone within a budget and guardrails. You move each agent up a level only when its track record earns it.

Example: in your first month you build the agent that reviews every ad set overnight. At first it only suggests. By month three it pauses losers and moves budget by itself within limits you set, and you only see what was decided and why.

❌ The old way: a media buyer checks the dashboards each morning, changes bids by hand and waits for the weekly report.

🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: you build and improve the agents that watch every ad set, page, webinar and email sequence around the clock. They spot what’s dropping, find the cause, fix it or launch a variant, and report what they did.

You give autonomy step by step: an agent can pause an ad on its own long before it can raise a budget. You decide where each agent stops and a human takes over.

Example: show-up rate drops on Tuesday’s webinar. Before anyone notices, an agent has found the cause (a reminder that never went out), fixed it and started testing a new reminder sequence.

❌ The old way: a creative team briefs an agency, waits two weeks and gets five ads.

🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: you build the agents that turn every live, interview and member story into hooks, ad cuts and shorts, that study what the best advertisers in the world are running, and that write in our voice.

Your taste becomes the eval: you write down what makes a great hook, a great cut and a great story, in rules and examples the agents check themselves against. Each time you reject something, the reason goes back into the rules.

Example: one webinar becomes dozens of hook variants by the next morning. You keep the best few, and next week the agents’ first drafts are already closer to your bar.

❌ The old way: an analyst rebuilds the numbers in a spreadsheet at the end of the month, and nobody trusts them.

🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: you build the agents that connect every touch to cash, from ad to lead, live, sale and transformed member, and that audit the tracking after every campaign.

No number, no test: you define the KPIs that matter (CAC, show-up, close rate, LTV, payback), and agents refuse to launch a test that isn’t wired to one.

Example: after each live, an agent cross-checks the ad platform, the CRM and our analytics, finds where they disagree and fixes the leak before the next live.

❌ The old way: lessons live in people’s heads and leave with them.

🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: every result goes back into the company brain, and agents read it before proposing anything. The machine never learns the same lesson twice.

You measure the machine itself: tests per week, time from idea to live, the share of the work done without a human, and how many agents moved up an autonomy level this month. You push those numbers up.

And always: no fake scarcity, no fake claims, real stories told with consent. The machine can scale, but it doesn’t decide what’s right. You do.

How you’ll know you’re AI-native: you spend your time building agents, writing evals and making calls, not doing the work by hand. Most experiments are generated and shipped by agents. The output grows every month while the headcount doesn’t.

You’ll own these KPIs: LTV / CAC ratio, funnel conversion rate by stage, experiments launched per week.

Desired outcomes: conversion rates 2x better than baseline, growth experimentation that runs continuously, a predictable growth engine.

Tools you’ll master: GA4, Optibase, Vidalytics, Clarity, Hotjar, Amplitude, Figma, Looker Studio, VWO, Optimizely, Claude Code, and whatever helps you see what others miss.

You have ideally a minimum of 3 years of experience in Conversion Rate Optimization, Growth Experimentation, or Performance Marketing, ideally within SaaS, e-commerce, or digital product environments.

You have a track record of designing, implementing, and scaling A/B and multivariate tests that have generated measurable improvements in revenue, user activation, or conversion.

You’ve built with AI and agents yourself: Claude Code, automations, APIs, evals, creative pipelines. Show us something you built, not a certificate.

A Conversion Architect, skilled at diagnosing funnel bottlenecks and translating data into structured experimentation roadmaps that deliver measurable business outcomes.

A Behavioral Strategist, fascinated by what drives human action, able to mix cognitive psychology, UX, and persuasion frameworks to design experiences that convert because they resonate.

A Data-driven Creator, fluent in GA4, Hotjar, AB Tasty, VWO, Amplitude, not just running tests, but connecting insights to revenue, retention, and lifetime value.

Loop thinker: you see every channel as a loop that can learn, and you can’t stop yourself from closing it.

Taste: you know a great hook in two seconds, and you’d rather ship one great ad than ten average ones.

Numbers-honest: you say when a test failed. You care about real revenue, not vanity metrics.

Builder, not manager: you’d rather build the system than coordinate an agency.

Growth over ego: you love hard feedback, you read, study and learn fast.

Cross-disciplinary: you move from psychology to spreadsheet to creative brief to code.

Analytical: you turn a vague problem into a clear hypothesis, a metric and an experiment.

English: Fluent English, you can hold a conversation on specific details with English-speaking colleagues.

#6992. Stopped-out student population reaches 37.8M, data finds

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

About 1.9 million people in this group left higher education recently, according to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center.

The stopped-out population, which represents nearly 1 in 5 working-age adults nationwide, has become an increasingly important pool of potential recruits as the sector confronts shrinking numbers of traditional-age students.

The majority of stopped-out students who return to higher education select new institutions to attend. Just over a third of returning students in the 2024-25 academic year, 34.4%, reenrolled at a college they previously attended, according to researchers.

One type of higher ed institution is particularly well positioned to benefit from returning students.

In 2023-24, public two-year colleges were the most popular type of institution for reenrolling stopped-out students who did not return to their original college. For example, 45.4% of students who previously attended a public four-year college enrolled at a community college in 2023-24, while just 18% returned to their original institution type.

Over half of students returning to higher ed, 53.2%, pursued an associate degree.

Stopped-out students were more likely to return to higher ed and earn a credential if they had completed a significant amount of coursework prior to disenrolling, according to the clearinghouse.

Among those who completed at least two years of full-time enrollment, 7.5% returned to college in the following decade, compared to 2.7% of the overall stopped-out population. And 8.5% earned a credential within their first year back, compared to 4.7% more broadly.

Most returning associate degree students enrolled in liberal arts and general studies programs, while bachelor’s students were most likely to pursue degrees in fields like business and management. Healthcare and the clinical sciences were the most popular fields for reenrolled students seeking an undergraduate certificate.

#6986. King Charles Had the Most Unexpected Response to Robert Pattinson Being Announced as James Bond

The royals have long been fans of the franchise.

King Charles and Queen Camilla had the best response to the long-awaited news that Twilight and Batman legend Robert Pattinson is set to become the new James Bond.

The royal family has long been associated with the iconic British spy series, with the King and Queen—along with Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales—attending the No Time to Die premiere at London’s Royal Albert Hall in September 2021 (the last film that was released in the long-running franchise).

In response to the official James Bond X account sharing the news about Pattinson, the royal family's account (which acts as a news source for the King and Queen), re-shared the post along with the comment: “Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond.”

So far, the quip has been liked over 250,000 times.

Prior to the 2021 premiere, the King had attended plenty of other screenings of the Bond series—dating as far back as 1981 for the launch of For Your Eyes Only, which had Roger Moore starring as the fictional MI6 agent.

The late Princess Diana and Princess Margaret also turned out for that particular premiere.

Commenting on his major career leap, Robert Pattinson said in a statement, “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime.”

He continued, “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Filming is expected to begin early next year, with an unspecified release date slated for sometime in 2028.

It will be the first James Bond movie produced by Amazon MGM, after the Broccoli family unexpectedly sold the rights in 2025.

CI/CD has been solved. Now it's being reinvented. AI agents don't just run pipelines. They write code, trigger builds, interpret failures, and propose fixes. The interfaces that developers use to understand and trust that work don't exist yet. We're building them.

At CircleCI, our guiding principles aren't posters on a wall. We learn fast: we run experiments, accept failure, and scale what works. We think like the customer: every decision connects back to the developer sitting in front of a failing build at 2 am. We own the outcome: not just our slice of it, but the whole thing. If that's how you already work, you'll fit here.

Every pipeline, job, and test that runs on CircleCI generates data, and that history is one of our biggest advantages in an agentic software delivery lifecycle. Flaky test detection, test insights, pipeline search, and agents that reason about why a build failed all depend on fast, reliable access to it.

The Query team owns the system that makes this possible. We pull product data out of the transactional services that create it and store it in datastores built for historical and analytical workloads. We serve it through domain-level APIs to CircleCI's product teams and to customers through our public API. Our goal is to make storing data "fire and forget" for every other team, and querying it fast and dependable at a scale that keeps growing.

You don't just patch problems, you ask why they happened. You'll fix the immediate issue, then solve the underlying team practice, process, or system that let it through.

You care about how data powers the product, not just where it lives. You know how to make a datastore fast at scale, and have tuned schemas and queries against real production load. You think like a platform engineer, measuring your work by how much it unblocks the teams building on it. AI isn't a tool you reach for occasionally; it's a core part of how you approach and solve problems. If that sounds like you, we want to talk.

#6981. “Sexy, Weirdo Bond”: Why Women Love Robert Pattinson’s Casting as 007

It feels like we might finally get a more vulnerable, less sexist James Bond.

Whether you were waiting with bated breath or not, the years-long wait to find out who the new James Bond is over, with the announcement that everyone’s fave Gen Z Robert Pattinson is set to take the reins.

In many ways, his casting is totally unsurprising—he is, seemingly, Hollywood’s only leading man right now, appearing in The Drama, The Odyssey, and Primetime this year alone (with Dune: Part Three still to come), on top of being literal Batman. And yet, at the same time, Rob as Bond feels like a break with tradition. I mean, he’s still a handsome straight white guy — but he’s not your typical alpha male.

There’s a silliness, darkness, and freakiness (complimentary) to Pattinson and the characters he’s played. With projects famously traversing both indie flicks and major blockbusters, he tends to appear as more fuckboy, weirdo, or Bond villain than the emotionally distant, hunky womanizer typically synonymous with 007. And women in particular seem to be into it.

I’m not just talking about women who grew up crushing on Cedric Diggory and Edward Cullen, either. Not to assign too much weight to the James Bond franchise, but Pattinson’s casting comes at a time when we’re grappling with what masculinity means today. In an era when misogynistic manosphere figureheads are as prevalent on our screens as Hollywood stars, there’s less appetite for clichéd portrayals of the archetypal alpha Bond guy, who’s super jacked, can’t express his emotions, and treats women like disposable objects.

For heterosexual women, this extends to our romantic lives, too. A new survey by female-led dating app Chyrpe found that over half of women wouldn’t actively look for an “alpha male” in a partner, with 70 percent saying they’d rather date a supportive, emotionally available man who’s happy to let them take the lead (Bond as a sub?!).

“The alpha male is traditionally understood as a man who is dominant, assertive, and accustomed to being in control,” says Gigi Engle, relationship expert for Chyrpe. “There’s an assumption that he’s emotionally self-sufficient, sexually dominant, and rarely, if ever, vulnerable. Psychologically, this represents a pretty narrow and restrictive understanding of masculinity.”

Despite what the manosphere would have you believe, this performance of masculinity doesn’t work for anyone involved. “When men feel they have to constantly be this ‘dominant’ character, there’s often very little room for emotional openness or genuine partnership,” continues Engle. “Women may simply be getting tired of having to accommodate someone else’s need to feel powerful. It’s boring, frankly.” In fact, the same Chyrpe survey found that 33 percent of men feel pressured by social media to embody the alpha male stereotype, while 30 percent say male friends ridicule them if they don’t take on an alpha role in their relationship.

There’s an opportunity, then, for macho franchises like James Bond to change things. “There’s a growing thirst for a masculinity that feels more human and less traditional,” says Engle. “For decades, popular culture has sold us the idea that an attractive man is someone who is powerful, emotionally restrained, physically strong, and always in control. But those expectations are starting to feel dated and lame. We’re becoming more interested in men who can hold complexity. We want guys who are comfortable with women who don’t need them to take charge.”

It feels like in Pattinson’s hands, we might see 007’s softer, nerdier, more emotional side—which could be a good thing for both men and women.

At least, that’s what a bunch of women I spoke to are hoping for. “He’s a James Bond you can see shooting the bad guys and also snuggling up in front of the telly watching Bridget Jones—and he’s kinda awkward,” says Clare.

Another Claire tells me: “I just cannot imagine him enthusiastically doing some of the cringier, misogynistic lines or scenes with female costars. I think he’ll be able to bring charisma, equally he doesn’t try to overpower his female costars. He holds his own in a scene without it ever needing to take anything away from the people he’s sharing that scene with.”

Nicole says a “different portrayal of masculinity would be nice,” but if we don’t get that, “he should be bisexual at least.”

Others, including Engle, are excited by the darkness Pattinson might bring to Bond. “He has an unconventional screen presence, to say the least,” she says. “There’s an introspective, slightly unpredictable quality to him that feels different from the traditionally hyper-masculine Bond we’ve become accustomed to. I’d love to see a Bond who retains the confidence, danger, and sexual charisma of the character but is allowed to have real emotions.”

Another woman I spoke to, Kitty, feels similarly: “First of all, [Pattinson] is my all-time crush, but I’m excited because I wonder if they’ll take the opportunity to make him darker and explore the theme of him being an alcoholic and reclusive. Similar to how he made Batman emo, will they make Bond more moody? Because so many people have explored how fucked up [Bond] actually is as a person, it would be cool to bring it to the front.”

Or, as Elise sums it up: “Let’s fucking go for sexy, weirdo Bond.”

Until the first film drops in 2028, we’ll have no idea how Pattinson will play Bond—but there’s no harm in projecting our emotionally intelligent fantasies onto him in the meantime.

#6978. Is There a Right Way to Respond to a Grammy Snub?

Artists like John Summit and MUNA have reacted to being shut out by the Recording Academy. But is there a correct way to approach it?

Not to go all “question for the culture” on everyone, but this year’s Grammy nominations have been on my mind for too long for me not to ask: Is there really a “right” way to acknowledge being snubbed by the Academy?

While the Recording Academy granted cultural aficionados the pleasant surprise of recognizing longtime underdogs like Raye, Remi Wolf, Tinashe, and Underscores, some names were noticeably absent from this year’s nominations list—and they had something to say about it.

For starters, EDM giant John Summit made headlines for his unfiltered reaction to being left out of the Dance and Electronic categories.

“never submitting to the grammys again unless shit changes, it’s all a fucking joke,” he wrote, criticizing the Academy for only recognizing “music industry fueled pop stars.”

After receiving backlash from online bystanders—including Charli xcx, who he previously requested to hop on a track in 2024—he walked back his claims, writing, “i realized i didn’t do a good job of making my point earlier. my intent was not to drag other artists down and i seriously congratulate everyone who was nominated. they fully deserve the recognition. i just think there should be an extra category for more dance music djs & producers.”

John isn’t wrong to point out the Academy’s standards in certain categories, but his delivery was a bit aggressive. Especially after he seemingly diminished fans’ opinions and deemed them “lil teeny bopper pop stan accounts with zero real world life experience.” It’s…a choice to say that about the people who move culture forward.

Naturally, his reaction got me thinking about the unspoken etiquette of addressing a snub. It’s valid to be upset over not being recognized by your peers, as well as seasoned vets in the biz. But you don’t want to ruin your chances for redemption, either.

Take Noah Kahan, for example. He reassured his fans that he’s “done everything I’ve ever needed to do in my career because of YOUR support” ahead of the nominations, only to be shut out in the core categories: Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Album of the Year. Though his album The Great Divide still earned a nod in the Best Contemporary Folk Album category, he acknowledged his snub with three words: “Life goes on.” Simple, yet effective!

Another artist who didn’t land a nod was pop princess and Cosmo cover girl Kim Petras, who made history as the first openly transgender woman to win a Grammy back in 2023. Her career took a tumultuous turn when she signed a major-label deal after riding the success of her award-winning track with Sam Smith, “Unholy.”

Years into her deal, she publicly accused her label of gatekeeping funds and resources, and pleaded to be released from her contract. She ultimately returned to her independent roots for her latest record, Detour, funding most of the studio sessions, visuals, and live performances herself. When the album didn’t earn a nod, fans claimed she was “snubbed,” since her hard work deserved recognition.

“I wouldn’t say so … I just left the industry tbh and I made the music to make the music cause I love it so much,” she wrote in response, claiming that her “nomination days [are] over” as she roots for Tinashe and Underscores.

The self-proclaimed “Greatest Band in the World,” MUNA, also started gaining momentum since trading a larger label for Phoebe Bridgers’ independent Saddest Factory Records in 2022. Their latest album, Dancing on the Wall, drew massive crowds at festivals like Lollapalooza and All Things Go last summer. The Academy has yet to acknowledge them, despite continued success.

The band’s lead singer, Katie Gavin, released a short video addressing fans after nominations dropped, saying, “I wasn’t expecting it, and I understand it. And it’s tough for a band like us because we make pop music, but we’re not as big as other pop artists.”

She added that they attempted to submit for alternative categories, but they ultimately didn’t make the cut because of their inherent pop sound. In the end, she kept things candid.

To put it plainly, there isn’t a definitive right or wrong way to go about being slept on. If artists decide to publicly address their snubs in the future, they should grab their pens and papers and take notes from Katie’s final sentiment.

“I’m really proud of all the people that did get nominated. There was so much amazing music this year,” she shared. “I hate being disappointed, but I’m not giving up hope.”
