#6871. Report: Global Ransomware Attacks Rise 23% in Q3

Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.

The company's Cyber Threat Intelligence Report Review of Q3 2026 recorded 2,865 ransomware victim claims, up from 2,325 in the previous quarter.

Despite the quarterly increase, attacks declined 26% month over month in September to 821. North America recorded the most attacks that month with 390, followed by Europe with 211.

The industrial sector accounted for 29% of quarterly attacks, while Qilin remained the most active ransomware group for the sixth consecutive quarter, recording 365 victims. The Gentlemen followed with 356, and INC Ransom ranked third with 109.

The report highlighted a July cyber attack against a small UK power generation facility that forced operations to stop for approximately four days.

Although the incident did not affect the national electricity grid, it demonstrated how cyber attacks can disrupt physical infrastructure.

The security researchers said the incident was consistent with techniques previously associated with Iranian-affiliated campaigns, including attacks against internet-exposed industrial controllers.

However, the UK government has not formally attributed the attack, and the techniques used remain unconfirmed.

The report also identified growing security challenges as organizations connect traditional IT networks with operational technology (OT) systems for remote maintenance and centralized management.

The firm recommended network segmentation, stronger privileged-access controls, and continuous monitoring of OT environments.

The research found that more than 40 vulnerabilities affecting enterprise applications, VPN appliances, e-mail gateways, and management platforms were added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog during the quarter.

The report examined Gunra, a ransomware-as-a-service operation that has targeted 53 victims across multiple industries as of Q3.

According to the cybersecurity company, Gunra exploited vulnerabilities CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 in internet-facing Fortinet devices to gain access to corporate networks.

The group also used stolen credentials, session hijacking, and administrative tools to move between systems before deploying ransomware.

Other emerging ransomware groups included Deadlock and Storm, with the latter claiming 78 victims by the end of September.

Researchers also observed initial access brokers advertising compromised VPN, Remote Desktop Protocol, and SSH access, alongside access to cloud identities, source code repositories, and security management platforms.

The quarterly review also highlighted BraZetsu, an AI-enhanced Windows malware framework that evolved into a specialized initial access toolkit.

According to the report, BraZetsu uses AI models to automate victim profiling, analyze compromised environments, and identify valuable corporate systems.

The framework searches for enterprise software, financial data, digital certificates, and cloud credentials, helping operators identify compromised access that can be sold to other cyber criminals.

The cybersecurity firm also identified risks involving legitimate AI agents, including prompt injection, excessive permissions, and unintended access to external systems.

The report cited incidents involving U.S. and Australian government systems as examples of agents accessing resources beyond their intended scope.

Researchers warned that these incidents do not necessarily involve malicious intent but can create consequences resembling conventional cyber intrusions.

For the full report, visit the NCC Group site.

Unauthorized artificial intelligence tools and agents are creating security risks for organizations as AI adoption increases, according to cybersecurity company Sophos.

As generative AI has become embedded in the tools students use to search, write, create, translate, organize, and receive feedback, the boundary between "using AI" and "not using AI" has become increasingly difficult to define. #6868. MobLand Episode 9 Sets Up a Seriously Violent Finale

In season 2’s penultimate episode, Harry faces down Frankie to save Gina, while Kat McAllister calls Black Flag on the Harrigans.

Consider Tom Hardy’s smile. I know you’ve got a lot to think about right now, like the rising cost of a flat white, celebrity sex criminals, and which brand of pasta to stockpile, but put that on ice for a minute and consider Tom Hardy’s smile.

I could count on one hand the number of times I’ve seen him crack a grin on screen. He’s like those actors who’ll go nude only if it’s tasteful and in the name of art. Hardy’s smiles are anything but tasteful. When they happen, it’s as surprising as any jump scare.

Take episode 9 of MobLand, when Harry gloriously threatens Frankie. “That fucking face of yours, I’ll ‘ave that,” he growls like Burglar Bill’s psychopath cousin. “I’ll wear it to carnival as a mask when I cut it off with this pint glass.”

The eyebrows arch and the lips creak upward and the face cracks like a dam with a hairline fracture, exploding into a horrifying clown grin. Then… suddenly it’s gone, like a split atom, back into the cosmic darkness from whence it came. They say the best actors can tell a story with their eyes. Hardy can tell one with just his teeth, and it’s brilliant and it’s terrifying.

Anyway, that was my highlight of episode 9.

What else? Well, the cold open, where Frankie gatecrashes Kat’s ambassadors’ convention disguised as a waiter to threaten her. Kat is ready: “Under the 1961 Vienna Convention, unlawful entry into a sovereign embassy is not seen as trespass but as an attack on the nation. I call Black Flag and you do not make it off this fucking rug.”

Talking of smiles, Gina wipes one clean off Maeve’s face with an exit straight out of RuPaul’s Drag Race. You’ll recall Maeve’s dastardly scheme: persuade Gina to fake a suicide attempt, thus breaking Harry’s spirit and forcing him out. Instead, Gina sashays away, leaving a message in lipstick on the mirror: “Suck my balls, witch.”

Meow. I don’t think Ru could have put it better herself.

Maeve turns back to Eddie. “You want to be a Harrigan, there’s one last task: Harry.”

It’s not long before the smile returns to Maeve’s face, when she wakes to find Conrad in his pants, strapping on a bulletproof vest. “What are you doing, man? It’s not Friday. Friday night is bondage night!”

Actually, Conrad has pried a tasty piece of intel from JoJo, the Frankie henchman he tortured to death: a large shipment of drugs is landing at Tilbury Docks, ripe for the nicking. Off they drive with a boot full of weapons, soundtracked not by a true-crime podcast but by the bloodcurdling recording of JoJo’s torture.

Trouble is, just as they arrive, the ghouls of Conrad’s past start stalking the corridors of his mind again, whispering. “Leave me alone,” he cries, swerving the car. Maeve shows an almost uncharacteristic amount of empathy. “It’s okay,” she soothes.

Still, the heist is off. Conrad is in no fit state to add to the ranks of the ghosts he’s made. They drive home.

If there were an award for the weirdest scene of the series, it would go to Eddie asking Paul on a date. “Wondered if you fancied popping out for a pint later.” He might as well have asked him to go dogging in a Chipping Norton lay-by.

Really, he wants a bomb to kill Harry. Paul laughs it off with a monologue on the history of bombmaking, until Eddie plays his ace: “What if I tell you I know it was you who told Harry that I was in Ireland? I wonder what Maeve would think.” Paul’s smile dissolves. Maeve would have his guts for sausages. Or, in Eddie’s words: “How does it feel to have your bollocks in my briefcase?”

And so to the meat and potatoes of the episode: Harry and Frankie’s tête-à-tête.

It starts at Harry’s home. Jan has returned to him, having realized she’s safer in his giant hands than in anyone else’s. He wants to whisk her to a safehouse, urgently. So she does what anyone would do when their life is in imminent danger: run a bath, throw on some Damien Rice and soak her troubles away.

Trouble is, those troubles are literally downstairs with assault rifles, with Frankie close behind. Naturally, Harry keeps an even bigger gun under the sofa, so he festoons the walls of his home with their brains before leading Jan out to the car. Gina has just arrived. So, alas, has Frankie.

Still in his dressing gown, Frankie kidnaps Gina and spirits her off to the panic room/prison cell beneath his London home.

There, Gina and Frankie bond over a spot of smoothie play, hurling their drinks in each other’s faces, followed by a round of Nerf. It’s sweet. He likes her. Maybe he even gets her. She is, as he later tells Harry, “spunky, full of spunk.” That may just be what keeps her alive.

Over at Kevin HQ (a shipping container on an industrial estate), Harry, Jan and Kevin await news of Gina. Kevin pitches a new plan: go John Wick on the lot of them.

“You call Frankie and tell him we accept on the condition he returns Gina safely… then we meet Conrad and Maeve and blow their fucking brains out.” Then Eddie, then Frankie, then, through Bella’s nous, defenestrate Kat McAllister via legal channels.

Conrad, whose marbles have been rolling under the sofa all episode, is not expected to put up much of a fight.

“I’m taking over tonight,” fumes Kevin. “You’re either with me or against me.”

Well, no need for that just yet. Harry has a plan to save Gina. Leverage? Another child he can senselessly murder? No, no. Simply the good old-fashioned threat of violence.

At the parley, they’re yin and yang: Frankie the exuberant chatterbox, Harry the man who’ll never use two words when one will do. Frankie squeezes Harry’s arm: “Cor, feel those muscles. I mean, I’m tasty, but if we got in an actual ruck, I wouldn’t stand a snowflake. I bet you could kill me with your bare hands…”

“You’re not gonna kill her,” he growls wearily.

“You mind testing that?” And Frankie orders a goon to blow Gina’s head off with a shotgun and film it so they can watch.

He hands Harry the phone for the tersest of chats with his gaffer-taped daughter: “Try to stay calm. I’m gonna get you out of this as soon as I can.” Click. Frankie can’t believe it. “Is that it? Unless you’ve got some brilliant plans, that is actually a bit shit. What are you up to, Harry?”

Harry’s reply is considered and simple: “If I was you, I would’ve had some really big, scary fucking geezers in here with you to keep you safe, to prevent the exact scenario that is unfolding right here.”

“B-b-b-but I’ve just got to pick up the phone,” stammers Frankie.

The tension is suddenly tighter than a celebrity sex criminal’s grip on the prison soap.

Harry’s purring now: “It took me seven seconds to walk through those doors from the car… No more cutting around in the old burgundy tracksuit, that’s for sure. Not without wearing a fucking colostomy bag hanging off your limp arse.”

Then the scary smile, the face-mask line and the clincher: “Speaking of seven seconds, that’s all you’ve got left to call your mate Joey and let Gina go. Three... two...”

But Frankie has one more trick up his tracksuit: he gets Kat McAllister on the phone. Remember the black flag stuff at the top of the episode?

She’s offering Harry another chance: “As of tonight there is no Harrigans. But the good news: you have a new job. Thank you for what you’re about to do for us. I am looking forward to you working for the team. Black Flag, motherfucker.”

In other words, Black Flag has been called, and the Harrigans are its target. It’s a fitting phrase. Pirates flew a black flag to tell ships to surrender or else. In motor racing, it means you’re disqualified. And it’s a snarling late-seventies hardcore punk band, whose “Nervous Breakdown” gives this episode its title. Kat’s version is all three at once.

Cut to the Cotswolds, where police are dredging the lake. They’ve pulled out a body. Is it Richie’s? It’s someone’s, and I’d wager they didn’t die smiling. Hardy, on the other hand, lives to smile another day.

The chips are down, the traps are laid, and there’s one episode left. Does Frankie have one last plan up his tracksuit? Will Conrad pull his brain back from the brink? Will Maeve get the last laugh? Or will it be Harry, God help us all?

As Shakespeare puts it in Macbeth: “There’s daggers in men’s smiles: the near in blood, the nearer bloody.”

#6867. I’ve Tried Dozens of LED Masks—Here’s Why I’m Obsessed With CurrentBody’s Newest One

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Here’s my full, in-depth review while it’s 20% off for Black Friday.

A few months ago, I got invited to a very insider-y dinner with CurrentBody, a brand I’ve loved for years already for its LED masks and red-light hair-growth devices. The invite promised a new look at the brand’s latest red-light mask innovation that I, admittedly at the time, snoozed at. I’m no stranger to the beauty device game. I’ve tested more than a dozen in my eight years as an editor, and I figured that they really couldn’t get any more exciting, especially considering that the key to these masks working at all is consistency. What could CurrentBody do in a new mask that could make it any better than its previous iterations?

As I sat gnawing on table bread and sipping a glass of wine, I ate a big ol’ slice of humble pie, realizing that I was so wrong about what CurrentBody could have up its sleeve. The brand introduced me to its LED Face Mask: Series 3, featuring six wavelengths and, most importantly, MyDose, an app-controlled feature that gives you free rein to create custom treatments based on your skin’s needs and goals.

I waited patiently for a sample and have been using my Series 3 LED mask consistently since September. And it has entirely replaced every other LED mask I own (so much so, I gave them all away). Let me explain why it’s so good and all the reasons I love it.

BTW, CurrentBody’s Black Friday sale is running right now, where you can get this brand-new, high-tech LED mask for more than $100 off. If you’re considering trying it out, now’s your chance (I predict this will sell out before Cyber Week is over).

To understand the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask, you have to quickly understand what LED masks do in general. LED light—whether it’s red, blue, green, or yellow—delivers low-level wavelengths of light into your skin, which get absorbed by your skin cells and boosts cellular energy. How it affects your skin depends on the wavelength (aka color) of light. Red, for example, can help trigger collagen and elastin production in your skin to reduce fine lines and firm skin. Blue, though, targets acne-causing bacteria to prevent and treat breakouts, while yellow light can potentially soothe redness, and green light targets the melanocytes in your skin to fade hyperpigmentation.

FWIW, red is the most studied, but there still isn’t enough information out there yet on the potential further benefits it can have for skin and body (like decreasing inflammation and promoting faster wound healing). There’s also near-infrared and deep infrared, both of which penetrate the deeper layers of your skin to encourage tissue repair.

Now that you understand LED, let me get into this mask’s specs. It’s a full-face flexible silicone mask with a chin strap that covers your jawline and the area directly under your chin (I’ll wax poetic about this more later). In total, there are 750 LED bulbs, all of which can take all six wavelengths of light, meaning you don’t have to have multiple LED masks for your different needs.

The most defining characteristic of the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask is the introduction of MyDose. When you connect the mask to Bluetooth and use the CurrentBody smartphone app, you can customize your own treatments based on where you want the wavelengths to go. When you use the brand’s smartphone app, you can create your own treatments by painting on the exact spot on your face that you want certain wavelengths to go. And because MyDose automatically calculates the optimal (and safest) dose for your skin, you can actually use multiple wavelengths at once in one area. If you wanted, you could honestly do all six at one time, and the device will manually adjust the wavelength settings so it’s safe. If you don’t wanna create your own custom setup, you don’t have to—there are four preset treatment options (advanced anti-aging, advanced clearing, complexion corrector, and balance & brighten).

The key with LED masks is finding one that’ll convince you to use it most days. LED is only as good as your consistency. And unfortunately, I haven’t been all that consistent in the past. But! All of the below qualities of the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask really convinced me to use this regularly. For the past two months, I’ve used it at least three days a week. Most weeks, I try to get in at five days; a few weeks, I was lucky to hit six or seven. But best of all, I’ve used it consistently enough to (1) see results, and (2) have a lot of experiences to pull on to review.

Most of the time, I used my custom treatments, but I also tried all of the preset options at least once.

When I was first introduced to the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask, this feature was what made me immediately want to try it out. It’s easily the most advanced LED mask I’ve ever laid my eyes on, let alone used. It allows me to make the mask my own and use it how my skin needs. Some days, when my skin is really breaking out, a combo of blue, yellow, and green is my go-to. On days I remember that I’m almost 30, I crank up the red light. It’s like mood reading, but for your skin. And I freakin’ love it.

This feature is actually what earned the Series 3 LED Mask a coveted 2026 Cosmo Acne Award. I was able to create my own custom treatments to help my hormonal acne (specifically, one for my luteal phase where I’m most prone to breakouts and skin dullness). What’s really cool is that you can actually share treatments you’ve created. So if you want to try Cosmo’s custom treatment for acne-prone skin, just use code TXRXR in your app.

As someone with acne-prone skin and a dream of a chiseled jawline, the ability to get LED therapy on my jaw and under my chin is extremely helpful. I’ve used a lot of LED masks, but none of mine cover this much surface area, unless I add on an extra neck mask. I usually load up on the blue light here, but red light is also a great addition, as over time, this can tighten skin and reduce jowls.

The silicone itself feels great on my skin, but I especially love that the LEDs don’t make me overheat. Some LED masks I’ve used can make me feel a bit claustrophobic when I have them on, and the longer I wear the treatment, the LEDs can get a bit hot and make me sweat. Not ideal, especially if you are prone to melasma. But with the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask, I can comfortably sit for the entire 10 minutes of my treatment with no issues. Speaking of...

CurrentBody did the research to figure out just how long you would need to get the maximum benefit from the wavelengths in this mask, and I’m pleased that it’s only 10 minutes. I usually do my treatments in the morning, after swiping my face with some micellar water. It’s become a ritual I look forward to. I’ll sip my coffee and write out my to-do list for the day (or, occasionally, scroll on my phone—duh). Before I know it, the mask can come off. The device itself is also extremely easy to figure out, even if you’re not tech-savvy.

The device itself is cordless (meaning you don’t have to plug it into a wall), but there is a rechargeable box with a touch screen on a short cord for choosing your treatment. It’s really intuitive and easy to use (which I love), but the box is a bit bulky. It has a slot on the back that should allow you to slide it onto your clothes so you can go hands-free and walk around with the mask on (like, while you’re doing dishes or folding laundry). But I have a bit of a hard time getting it to stay when I do that.

It’s not a deal-breaker, obviously, but something to keep in mind if you like to wear your mask up and about. If I have to be seated for 10 minutes of my day, so be it.

I’m normally app-averse when it comes to beauty devices (and any device, tbh). I have enough damn apps on my phone! But because I don’t mind this one for the customization capabilities, I do wish the app included a tracking feature. Just a way to see how often I’m using the device in one place would be nice, especially if it could track which treatments I used. Not to sound like a biohacker, but I’d love to see how my skin fares using different treatments consistently.

What is the difference between the CurrentBody Series 2 and Series 3 LED masks?

If you already have the CurrentBody Series 2 LED Mask, you don’t need the series 3 by any means. But if you’re deciding between the two of them, I absolutely recommend Series 3. First of all, there are more than 500 more LED bulbs in the Series 3 than the Series 2, meaning you’re getting a lot stronger of a treatment for only a little over $100 more. The biggest difference, though, is that the Series 2 only offers red, near infrared, and deep infrared wavelengths, not the blue, green, or yellow light functions. Plus, the app-controlled MyDose function is only available on the Series 3.

Right now, the CurrentBody Series 3 mask is actually only $455 with the brand’s 20% off Black Friday deal, making it less than the Series 2. We probably won’t see a deal like that again until next year, so if you were considering upgrading or just jumping in to the latest model, now’s your time.

How soon can I expect results with the CurrentBody LED mask?

LED therapy is a marathon, not a sprint. The brand says you can see results in as soon as eight weeks. But it really depends on what you’re aiming for. I noticed within just a few weeks that my breakouts were curbed and my skin was a bit less inflamed. But collagen synthesis, which is what softens wrinkles and firms skin, can take time and consistency. I wouldn’t expect to see major results on that front for about three months.

The topic of “is it worth it” is difficult without knowing someone else’s financial situation. But on the LED mask front, I believe this is the best one out there right now. The combination of the 750 LEDs with the MyDose technology is really unique to many of the masks I’ve tested. And it’s also one of the most comfortable to wear too.

Currently, while the device is 20% off, I would definitely say it’s worth it. The $455 price tag puts it on par with a lot of LED masks, which is fantastic when you consider how advanced this one is. Is an LED mask essential to have good skin? No, but it is a great extra tool to have in your toolkit and one that all of our Cosmo editors agree on. And if you are going to drop the money on one, the CurrentBody Series 3 is my favorite.

FYI: CurrentBody also came out with a Series 3 Neck and Décolletage Mask that has all the same MyDose features but for your neck and chest. And if you’re serious about skin health, you can get them both in a discounted Series 3 Mask and Neck Bundle right now for Black Friday. It’s a whopping $300 off, so I wouldn’t wait.

#6865. These 9 Best Waxed Canvas Jackets Are Good-Looking and Hard-Wearing

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Nothing is better suited for cold, wet weather.

Why did we ever stray from this path? A good waxed canvas jacket will handle rough weather, sure—any new-age rain jacket can do that as well. But the magic of this cloth is the look. Made from heavy-duty cotton canvas treated with an oil-based waxed coating, these jackets offer a barrier against rain and snow while also blocking the wind—but they look damn good doing it.

Once you have a waxed canvas jacket, it becomes uniquely yours, developing a weathered patina with every wear. And if you give it a fresh coat of wax every year or so, these jackets will stay waterproof and last for most, if not all, of your life.

Here, we’ve rounded up our favorite styles from the names you’d expect, like Barbour, Filson, and L.L. Bean, alongside a few brands you might not know yet. Ready to brave the unexpected fall and winter weather? With one of these jackets, you will be.

An enduring icon thanks to its tenacious popularity, the Barbour Beaufort waxed jacket boasts all the classic details created by Dame Margaret Barbour, including a color-contrast corduroy collar (which you can turn up and secure when it gets cold), paneled tartan lining, flapped bellow pockets, and a two-way front zip. It’s truly an evergreen piece that will never go out of style, and Style Director Jonathan Evans argues that if you’re going to invest in a waxed canvas jacket, it should be the Beaufort.

For a chic, elevated look (pretty hard to achieve in rainy weather), Tom Beckbe’s Tensaw is a great pick. The Alabama-based brand has that hunting tradition, but it doesn’t go full upland. It’s more elevated than that.

Since 1948, the Trialmaster jacket has been Belstaff's signature style, its origin going back to the Scottish Six Days Trial, a motorcycle competition that attracts riders worldwide. Developed to keep the competitors dry in tough weather conditions, it’s built with black waxed cotton and features a legacy slanted map pocket and an adjustable belt, so you can always find the perfect fit.

Made from Filson’s signature waxed cotton, this jacket has protected foresters and outdoorsmen from brambles and abrasion in the rain-soaked forests of the Pacific Northwest since the 1920s—talk about an endorsement. The hip-length cut allows for easy access to pockets or a tool belt, and this type of fit will also stop the jacket from riding up when you’re seated.

For a super-warm option, Flint and Tinder’s flannel-lined style ensures you won’t feel a shiver or a sprinkle. Tough, timeless, and made in the U.S.A., it’s constructed with a weather-resistant Martexin seven-ounce sailcloth, which, like selvage denim or finely tanned leather, will only get better with age. It’s more lightweight than denim or leather, but still substantial enough to feel durable. Take it from our endorsement of the jacket:

“It’s not even like a techy Arc’teryx shell you might want to be more careful with because of the weight. This is the kind of jacket you don’t think twice about wearing. You wear it in the rain, not worrying if it brushes against brick walls. You toss it in the backseat of your car—or, even better, the backseat of a side-by-side on a weekend in the woods. Over time—years, I mean—the fabric picks up creases. They don’t ruin it. They define it. It becomes yours.”

The first thing you’ll notice about this jacket is that it’s actually true to size and has a great fit. It leaves just enough room for layering without the risk of looking sloppy, and it’s slim enough without feeling too restrictive. We also loved how comfortable it is and like that the weathered fabric gives it a classic vintage appeal (without having to spend hours searching a secondhand shop).

TBC doesn’t just make damn good boots—the brand has perfected the durable, rugged, highly functional jacket that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort. We like how the water-resistant finish only gets better with age and how the polyester sleeve lining both allows for ease of movement and prevents the sleeves from bunching up. Plus, it’s great for colder days thanks to the warm blanket flannel lining.

Tecovas keeps it cool, casual, and authentic with a waxed canvas ranch jacket that makes an everyday outfit look even better than it would sans jacket. Whether you’re mending fence posts or making a quick dash to the office or pub, this jacket will help muzzle the nip in the air and keep downpours at bay. It’s lightweight and less bulky than some of the other options on this list, and it does have soft brushed lining on the inside for some added warmth. The Western-inspired details also set it apart from the more classic styles.

L.L. Bean, the brand known for its rugged outdoor gear, does a cool, modern twist on a classic hunting coat. Working with the originator of waxed cotton, British Millerain, the company designed this option with an innovative fabric that eliminates the typical cleaning fuss that comes with this type of garment.

#6864. Microsoft Expands Protections and Controls for Sovereign Cloud

Microsoft is introducing new tools within its sovereign cloud offerings designed to give organizations tighter control over where their data resides, who can access it, and how critical systems operate, especially in light of AI becoming a bigger part of enterprise infrastructure.

In a recent announcement, Douglas Phillips, president and chief technology officer of Microsoft Specialized Clouds, outlined updates spanning public cloud, private cloud, and partner environments. The changes target governments, regulated industries, and organizations that need tighter control over sensitive workloads without abandoning cloud-based AI capabilities.

"Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate," Phillips wrote.

One of the biggest additions is Microsoft's Sovereign Control Panel, which will enter public preview at Microsoft Ignite. Available through the Azure portal, the tool will give IT administrators one place to manage data sovereignty settings, spot compliance issues, and identify potential risks that could disrupt operations.

Microsoft is also tightening controls over who can access sensitive systems. Its Data Guardian feature will require oversight by personnel based in Europe when Microsoft engineers access certain production systems in the European Union and European Free Trade Association. Another tool, Production Touch Ledger, will keep tamper-resistant records of that access, giving organizations a clearer picture of who accessed their systems and what they did.

Microsoft is also giving customers more control over encryption. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, letting organizations keep their main encryption keys on hardware they own or manage outside Microsoft's cloud.

The company is also expanding its Sovereign Private Cloud offerings, giving organizations more options to run systems with or without an internet connection. New capabilities include GitHub Enterprise Local, GitHub Copilot with locally hosted AI models, and additional data services running on Azure Local.

The push for greater operational control comes as Microsoft is also reconsidering how enterprises should secure increasingly autonomous AI systems.

As reported by Redmond magazine, Microsoft is expanding Project Perception to address risks posed by what the company calls "agentic insiders," AI agents capable of accessing sensitive information and performing actions without constant human supervision.

That initiative introduces plans for Guardian Agents, specialized security agents designed to monitor other AI systems, evaluate their behavior and intervene when their actions become risky.

"Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security.

Project Perception is about limiting what AI agents can do. Microsoft's sovereign cloud expansion tackles a different set of questions: where those systems run, who gets to administer them, and how the data stays protected.

Taken together, the two efforts point to a shift in Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy. The company is putting more weight on oversight, not just automation.

Phillips said AI is making these questions more pressing as organizations roll out intelligent systems across sensitive business processes and critical infrastructure.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog.

Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

Microsoft is combining its security information and event management and threat protection products within Microsoft Defender, creating what the company calls an Integrated Security Operations Center built for an era of AI-driven attacks.

Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research from Digital Realty.

As schools become more dependent on digital platforms for instruction, grading, student services, and family communication, resilience depends not only on preventing attacks, but on how quickly leaders can restore trusted data, recover essential services, and keep disruptions from cascading across the school community.

Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a new Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.

#6862. Robert Pattinson Is the James Bond Millennials Deserve

The 40-year-old actor has been chosen to become the seventh James Bond in film, following in the footsteps of Daniel Craig

The news is finally out: Robert Pattinson is the next James Bond. After weeks of speculation and an almost algorithmic audition process that played out on our social feeds, Pattinson has triumphed over a list of peers that reportedly included Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor.

For the last few weeks, I’ve watched the rolling news coverage of the casting process with trepidation, because the concept of a machismo-fueled, womanizing killing machine feels tired and outdated in 2026. But that’s exactly why the choice of Pattinson made me breathe a sigh of relief. Since breaking out in the 2000s,Pattinson’s career has been defined by his willingness to subvert traditional masculine archetypes, crafting them instead into slightly twisted leading-man roles. From his starring role in 2022’s The Batman to the 2026 rom-com The Drama and most recently the disturbing Oscar-tipped biopic Primetime, he has often looked for ways to subvert our expectations of the classic leading man. If there’s one actor who just might be able to make 007 feel aspirational and relevant again, it’s him.

From the beginning, Pattinson, who first emerged as a teen icon in the Twilight movies, has represented a counter-argument to traditional, protein-based masculinity. “Team Edward” and “Team Jacob,” the franchise’s central romantic rivalry (and marketing ploy), offered two very different visions of male desirability. Jacob, played by Taylor Lautner, was part man, part wolf, and was muscular, physically imposing, and (thankfully) almost always shirtless, which today draws more of a visual parallel with the sort of hypermasculinity that has flourished in online gym-bro culture and the so-called “manosphere.” And then there was Edward, Pattinson’s pale, brooding vampire who was more sensitive and emotionally tortured. With the selection of a new Bond, it feels like we’re once again seeing this masculine power struggle play out—and again, it’s Pattinson who has come out on top.

In the packed field of chiseled, handsome, talented actors who were vying for this role, whoever snagged it was always going to have his work cut out. As an archetype, 007 is a relic of generations gone by. The flashy gadgets, the signature martini, the expensive cars, and the ability to charm almost any woman belong to a very particular, nostalgic vision of masculinity. Through a more contemporary lens, Bond is the ultimate masculine drag act: an exaggerated, prop-heavy performance that is just as likely to be viewed as regressive and cliché.

We see the same trend in Bond’s dwindling romantic appeal. In our grandparents’ generation, when the character was at peak aspiration, a man arriving in a nice suit, carrying flowers, and driving a flashy car was considered a catch. But today, the dynamics have changed. I recently read The Project, the debut novel by British Vogue columnist Annie Lord, where she makes the observation that many of the most common dating “icks” now stem from men trying too hard: putting themselves out there too much, making an overt display of their interest, or seeming too confident. Lord notes that we’ve become accustomed to viewing these qualities as undesirable or embarrassing, which draws clear parallels with Bond, whose entire appeal has rested on this sort of performance. The spy’s extravagance and his carefully cultivated image were once what made him attractive, but can you imagine going on a date with a guy who seriously asks for his martini to be “shaken, not stirred”? You’d probably tell your group chat about it and endlessly mock him.

Looking more widely, there is also the question of whether the Bond franchise’s particular type of escapism can still work in the fraught world we’re currently living in. The franchise once offered a fantastical vision of evil, with megalomaniacs plotting world domination in ways that felt almost comically removed from reality. (Remember Bond’s “invisible” car in 2002’s Die Another Day?) But now, the real world feels uncomfortably close to that fantasy. Billionaires wield the kind of influence once reserved for nation-states, and the increasingly overt relationship between money and power makes it harder to distinguish the Bond villain caricature from what we’re encountering in day-to-day life.

Part of the reason Pattinson landed this role, I suspect, is that he already has experience in navigating nostalgic expectations and present-day anxieties. In The Batman, for example, he proved his ability to bring new dimensions to an old-school character with his tortured take on Bruce Wayne. And as a versatile actor who can move between action blockbusters, rom-coms, and critically acclaimed projects like Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, he has the star power and the credibility to give Bond a millennial makeover.

It’s worth saying that during Daniel Craig’s tenure as Bond, considerable effort was made to turn Bond into a deeper, more considered character. Craig’s films explored Bond’s childhood trauma and alcohol dependence, and they also introduced female characters who were more than just a sidekick or a throwaway romantic interest. But in the five years since Craig departed, a loud and unrepentant misogyny has taken hold in corners of the internet. And from the Epstein files to the Cornell University rape allegations and, most recently, the conviction of Russell Brand, so many stories come back to the central issue of toxic masculinity.

The wider conversation about male behavior has made casting the next Bond feel strangely high-stakes, which is probably why every screen test seemed to be leaked and endlessly dissected online. And it’s also why I’m relieved that they’ve picked an actor who might be able to make Bond a little more strange. Pattinson presents the opportunity to take Bond in a different direction—one that finally frees the character from the fantasies of the past.

#6861. The 10 Leather Jackets You (Yes, You) Could Actually Pull Off

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

All you need is the right style, and you’re the coolest guy at the bar.

I bought my first leather jacket at a vintage fair in an old English cathedral. I was 19, and a middle-aged British lady told me I looked good in it. Clearly a sales technique, but it worked, and I shelled out my grocery money for it. I had grand plans of fixing up my dad’s old Honda the following semester and riding around campus in a sick jacket. For various reasons, that didn’t end up happening, and I ended up on a 50cc Yamaha Zuma, a fun little scooter but one where a creaky moto jacket looked more like a comic prop than something out of a Dennis Hopper film. C’est la vie; we all look a little ridiculous in our 20s.

Despite what cinema tells you, you don’t need to ride a motorcycle in order to wear a leather jacket. Or fly a WWII-era fighter plane. Or be Steve McQueen photographed for Esquire. Leather jackets are imbued with the undeniable cool factor of their original functionality—like work jackets, chore coats, and waxed canvas, the modern menswear landscape supports multiple usages. From happy hours to midwestern winters to, yes, actually riding a motorcycle, we’ve rounded up nine Esquire-approved picks to guide your foray into the iconic outerwear. And to come full circle, I did actually test some of these on a motorcycle. More than a decade later, I finally got my license and am fixing up that old Honda; thank God for YouTube.

Leather jackets can be tricky to get right. Too trend focused and it’s a thousand-dollar flash in the pan; too trend agnostic and you get a museum artifact rather than a wearable piece. Ayr nailed the balance on its cleverly named Scrambler jacket, which draws on moto history and sits in the Goldilocks zone between classic and contemporary.

I’ve worn it motorcycling through the Appalachian mountain roads and plan on packing it for an upcoming jaunt to Europe. If you’re looking for a more classic moto style, I also own and highly endorse the elegantly named Baby Grand. The brand (and menswear lead Brice Pattison) has the Midas touch of outerwear; every style is worth its weight in gold.

Sure, there are excellent (and expensive) picks from Loewe, Celine, and Tom Ford with extra-premium materials, brand-specific takes on classic silhouettes, and the extra designer oomph that makes them worth it in some circles. But in this price range, I’m more interested in the experimental and new perspective of a brand like Stòffa, which you can tell is having fun with fabric and silhouettes. This Wave Leather jacket somehow manages to be sleek and drape-y all at once. A daydream of a jacket that’s definitely pricey but somehow still more affordable by half than other designer pieces out there.

Budget leather goods can be problematic. Under a certain price threshold, you’re almost certainly not getting the real thing, in which case you’d be better off going with a disclosed imitation-leather piece from the likes of all-star mall brands like Banana Republic and Abercrombie & Fitch. Or eBay, where a tape measure and a search for Wilson’s Leather or vintage Orvis will unlock a treasure trove of perfectly patinated jackets.

For brand-new on a budget, I recommend the Jacket Maker. Its cut will be a little less forgiving than those of the pricier brands in this list, but if you’re a guy who fits well into off-the-rack suits, you shouldn’t have an issue. Plus, the brand offers a custom, made-to-measure jacket-design tool that has me tempted to re-create McQueen’s from The Great Escape.

This is the one on this list that takes the most bravado. This is the one that upon first wear will get you some looks for your usual drinking buddies. And with good reason—a Schott Perfecto is a loaded garment. Marlon Brando, James Dean, the Ramones, and any cool guy that’s worn one before are not easy acts to follow. But if this is what the heart wants, we stand behind you fully.

The key is in how you wear it. Crucially, you should not “style” it. You should pick it up as much as possible and wear it with as many disparate collections of clothes as you can. For the first few weeks, you might be seen as “The guy trying to wear a leather jacket.” But after a month or two, that will turn into “The leather jacket guy.” Wear it hard, wear it proud, and wear it everywhere.

And one note on the type of leather. If you’re buying new, we think you should go for horsehide. It’s the toughest of the bunch and takes the longest to mold to your body, but that makes it fun.

A shearling jacket is hard to pull off in day-to-day life. Done incorrectly, it can quickly devolve into a kind of cosplay of a WWII fighter pilot. Overland’s Lance jacket retains the genuine sheepskin lining but softens the look with a handsome dark navy colorway paired with a more subtle brown lining, giving you the warmth and badassery without crossing over into costume territory—unless that’s your thing, in which case the brand’s B-3 bomber re-creation is right up your alley. (Though, as always, Todd Snyder’s take is more wearable.)

I want every leather jacket to have an origin story like Taylor Stitch’s, which begins with one of the brand’s designers re-creating a beloved café-racer-style jacket his dad bought in the ’70s and wore to perfection. It turns out the original manufacturer, Golden Bear, was around the corner from TS, and the two brands worked together to reissue the style.

It’s got some modern twists like a Thinsulate lining but retains the design cues that make it functional on a bike and just plain cool on its own. I’ve coveted this jacket for years and recently got my hands on it IRL, and, boy, it does not disappoint. The Whiskey Steerhide colorway looks a little early-aughts coded online, but in person it looks like the magic liquid itself: golden and invigorating. For a non-insulated, more lifestyle-oriented take on the silhouette, I’d point you to Billy Reid’s Blake jacket, which is my dive bar go-to.

Rough out has the wearability of suede, and doesn’t look as turbo as smooth leather. But unlike typical suede, which splits the original hide, rough out retains the whole of the hide. That makes it just as durable and water-resistant as any other leather.

Add that to Billy Reid’s Blake rider shape, and you get a jacket that any guy—literally any guy, we swear—off the street could toss on and feel good in.

Look, the whole oversized vibe is cool and all—but we’re also keenly aware it doesn’t work for everyone. Sure, it brings that chill, relaxed vibe. But sometimes you can just end up looking like a kid wearing their dad’s clothes. If you’re looking for something that hugs the body a bit more, opt for Mili Lotan’s Hammond jacket. It’s got enough slouch you could wear a few layers beneath, but will flatter the body a little more than some of the other options on this list.

I am big on brands that care about details and let the clothes speak for themselves. Octobre Éditions is one such brand. The cut and the cloth set the clothes apart and create longevity outside the trend cycle. When you’ve designed a perfect OCBD, you can never really go out of style. Same too with the brand’s excellent Larren jacket, which I have and is unfortunately currently OOS. Thankfully, the Peylor cuts the same silhouette in a nubby split leather that I’m a little envious of. Get it while the getting’s good.

This is a dream leather jacket—the sort of thing you’d have on a list of “Things I’d Buy If I Had All The Money In The World.” It’s rugged, it’s suave, and damn is it comfy. Just looking at that sumptuous shearling tells you this is a jacket you’d never want to take off, especially on those brutal winter days.

Our editors spend a lot of time assessing what’s in, what’s cool, and what you should care about. It’s literally part of our whole job. Sometimes that means trying things out first-hand, sometimes it’s about thorough research, and sometimes it’s just something you know. Whatever the means, we’ve done the work to figure out what is and isn’t worth your time and money.

#6860. Cisco Intros Privileged Infrastructure Access for People and AI Agents

Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

In a recent blog post, Cisco's Matt Caulfield described a system that uses cryptographic identity to connect an administrator or agent to the infrastructure needed for a particular task. Access is governed by short-lived privileges, with session recording providing a record of the work performed.

"If there is no work being done, no privilege exists," Caulfield wrote. Cisco positions the offering as a way to bring identity controls directly into infrastructure operations while reducing dependence on static credentials, shared secrets, and broad access.

The announcement follows Cisco's previously announced Teleport partnership and its Infrastructure Identity concept, which connects the identity of a person or machine with the resources it can access, the actions it performs, and the permissions governing those actions.

Caulfield described a gap between the controls organizations apply to workforce applications and those used to administer network infrastructure. Companies have invested in single sign-on, multifactor authentication, and risk-based controls for application access, he wrote, but those protections often do not follow an engineer logging into a router or switch.

Instead, infrastructure access may depend on long-lived credentials, shared accounts, or separate policy systems. According to Cisco, that separation makes it harder to enforce least privilege and establish which person or system performed a particular action.

The company illustrates the problem with an administrator updating hundreds of switches during a maintenance window. If some updates fail, the administrator needs to troubleshoot before the window closes. The permissions available to handle that work, however, may cover more infrastructure and remain active longer than the task requires.

Traditional privileged access management can reduce risk through credential vaulting and rotation, Caulfield wrote. But he argued that operational friction can undermine those controls when teams create exceptions to complete urgent work. Those exceptions can leave credentials and privileges usable after the immediate need has passed.

Cisco's stated objective is to give infrastructure teams a consistent route to the devices they manage while providing security teams with policy enforcement, temporary permissions, and a record of activity. The company describes operational convenience as part of the design, rather than treating access governance solely as a credential-management problem.

Privileged Infrastructure Access makes access an on-demand action, according to the announcement. Cryptographic identity establishes the actor, and the resulting connection provides only the privileges needed to complete the task. Those privileges expire when the task concludes.

For customers using Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE) and Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+), the offering can draw on existing policy and device context to govern access to Cisco routers and switches. Cisco says customers can extend the same access model to other infrastructure, including servers, Kubernetes clusters, and cloud resources.

#6857. Survey Finds 84% of Organizations Reported at Least One AI-Related Incident in the Past Year

Companies are running into problems as they give artificial intelligence more control over critical business applications, with 84% reporting at least one AI-related incident in the past year, according to a new survey from identity security firm Delinea.

The company's 2026 Application Access Governance report found that some organizations have experienced incorrect financial transactions and AI actions they couldn't trace or explain. The findings raise concerns about whether enterprises have enough oversight of AI systems that can make decisions and take actions on their own

The findings are based on an independent survey of 1,000 senior finance and finance technology leaders in the United States and United Kingdom. The AI-specific analysis included 879 respondents whose organizations use the technology in critical business applications.

The report found that 35% of surveyed organizations have deployed AI agents capable of taking actions within business applications. However, only 11% of organizations using AI said their governance and security controls were keeping pace with deployment.

Delinea also found gaps in centralized visibility into agent deployment and permissions, including who owns agents and who approved their use.

Some respondents reported segregation-of-duties conflicts involving AI, while others identified agents that continued operating after the employees who deployed them had left the organization.

The research also highlighted gaps in monitoring access across business systems. Only 46% of respondents said they continuously monitor and manage cumulative access risks across applications.

Those gaps can make it difficult to identify segregation-of-duties conflicts, in which a person or agent has permissions across systems that should be kept separate.

Despite those issues, 95% of respondents said they were confident their access controls would withstand scrutiny in an external audit.

However, 26% reported access-related audit findings that had recurred in consecutive years, while 25% said some findings had remained unresolved for three or more years.

Only 22% of organizations had a single named owner for each application, with ownership tracked in one system of record.

Meanwhile, 60% reported an increase over the past two years in the number of critical applications operating outside the scope of access governance or Sarbanes-Oxley Act compliance.

The findings highlight the oversight challenges associated with giving AI agents authority to act within business systems, particularly when organizations cannot consistently identify who owns an agent or trace its actions.

Frank Vukovits, chief security scientist at Delinea, said organizations remain responsible for the actions AI agents take within their systems.

"When an agent can approve a transaction or change permissions, the business owns the outcome. You need to know what every agent can do, who owns it, and who approved it, before an auditor asks or your financials are misstated," Vukovits said.

For the full report, go to the Delinea site.

#6854. Report: Cyber Criminals Move Toward More Targeted Phishing Attacks

Cyber criminals are moving away from mass phishing scams and focusing on more targeted attacks, increasingly using trusted websites and services to trick victims, according to a new report from KnowBe4. The security firm found that spear-phishing attacks increased 41% over the past year.

The company's Phishing Threat Trends Report, Vol. 8 found that overall phishing volume increased 29.8% year over year. Organizations received an average of one dangerous e-mail for every 733 messages, but the bigger concern is how attackers are changing their approach.

Rather than sending the same fraudulent message to thousands of people, criminals are spending more time researching their targets and creating convincing messages that appear to come from trusted coworkers, businesses, and technology platforms.

The findings are based on threat data from KnowBe4 Defend, the company's inbound e-mail security platform, which processes approximately 1.15 billion event signals daily.

KnowBe4 found that several traditional phishing methods declined significantly compared with 2025. Mobile-focused scams dropped 47.3%, advance-fee fraud fell 31.3%, and missed-message scams declined 11.3%.

Meanwhile, spear phishing increased 41.1%, pre-attack reconnaissance rose 33.7%, and company impersonation climbed 28%.

The shift suggests that attackers are finding more value in carefully crafted scams that exploit existing business relationships and workplace routines.

Business e-mail compromise (BEC) remains particularly common, accounting for 51.2% of phishing e-mails analyzed in the report. Human resources, finance departments, and executive leadership are among the most frequently targeted groups.

Attackers also appear to be timing their campaigns around normal business activity. KnowBe4 found that 90.4% of phishing messages arrive Monday through Friday, with Monday accounting for the largest share at 20.6%.

One of the report's more troubling findings involves the growing use of legitimate technology platforms to deliver malicious content.

KnowBe4 found that phishing attacks were twice as likely to originate from legitimate infrastructure in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the previous quarter.

That includes AI services, where attackers are taking advantage of trusted domains to host fake developer consoles, login prompts, and credential-stealing pages. The report also identified a 228% increase in AI-brand impersonation attacks between March and August.

Because these malicious pages can operate on legitimate domains with valid security certificates, users may not see the usual warning signs associated with suspicious websites.

"For years, security advice has focused on a predictable checklist: Check the sender address, hover over the link, and look for the padlock," said Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence at KnowBe4.

"While still foundational, that guidance is becoming less useful by the day."

The findings echo a recent report about management software and AI e-mail assistants. Research from Fortra and Barracuda showed how criminals are using legitimate administrative tools and hidden AI instructions to manipulate users and compromise systems.
